cover.title: Why Didn't We Buy Less Gas?

lines.text: In 2022, gas jumped 31%. Americans barely bought less.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-two, gas jumped thirty-one percent. Americans barely bought less.

lines.text: Gas averaged $3.01 a gallon in 2021, then $3.95 in 2022.
lines.say: Gas averaged three dollars and one cent a gallon in twenty twenty-one, then three dollars and ninety-five cents in twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: Yet US gasoline use fell less than 1%. Why?
lines.say: Yet US gasoline use fell less than one percent. Why?

lines.text: Part of the answer is price elasticity: % change in amount bought ÷ % change in price.
lines.say: Part of the answer is price elasticity: percent change in amount bought, divided by percent change in price.

lines.text: Hypothetical: gas goes from $4.00 to $4.40, up 10%. Weekly gallons drop from 10 to 9.9, down 1%.
lines.say: Say gas goes from four dollars to four dollars and forty cents, up ten percent. Weekly gallons drop from ten to nine point nine, down one percent.
Minus one divided by ten is minus zero point one. That's inelastic: buyers barely react.

lines.text: So the weekly bill rises from $40.00 to $43.56, and sellers collect more.
lines.say: So the weekly bill rises from forty dollars to forty-three dollars and fifty-six cents, and sellers collect more.

lines.text: Cigarettes too: a 10% price rise cuts cigarettes smoked only about 3 to 5%.
lines.say: Cigarettes too: a ten percent price rise cuts cigarettes smoked only about three to five percent.

lines.text: No quick substitute, so people keep buying as prices climb.
lines.say: No quick substitute, so people keep buying as prices climb.

post.title: Gas jumped 31% in 2022. Why we barely bought less
post.ig:
In 2022, US gas prices jumped 31%. Americans barely bought less.
Regular gas averaged $3.01/gal in 2021 and $3.95 in 2022, while US gasoline use fell less than 1% (EIA).
That's price elasticity: % change in amount bought divided by % change in price. Hypothetical: price +10%, gallons -1% = -0.1, inelastic, and the weekly bill rises from $40.00 to $43.56.
Cigarettes too: a 10% price rise cuts cigarettes smoked about 3-5%.
Sources: EIA retail gasoline prices and consumption data; National Cancer Institute Monograph 14; CDC.
